scope: CBSE Class 6 Science · Curiosity · Chapter 6 · Materials Around Us
claimBoundary: Deterministic readiness validation using synthetic learner scenarios only. This is not a live student study, school pilot, efficacy trial, attainment claim, chemical-safety certification, laboratory accreditation or permission for hazardous material-identification experiments.
passRule: Every scenario must map to an implemented Chapter 6 topic, a Kiki misconception/remediation path, at least one linked reasoning or mastery assessment, a privacy-safe learner action and an observable mastery criterion while preserving the no-tasting, known-safe-sample, non-destructive-tool and eye-safety boundaries.

scenarios.need: Learner treats an object name and a material name as interchangeable, for example calling a spoon itself a material.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Use teacher-provided labelled object cards to separate WHAT THE OBJECT IS from WHAT IT IS MADE FROM, then identify examples where one object type can use different materials and one material can be used for different objects.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Correctly distinguishes object identity from material identity in unfamiliar card examples and explains at least one many-to-many object/material relationship without dismantling any real object.

scenarios.need: Learner changes the grouping rule midway or assumes that similar colour and appearance prove two objects are made from the same material.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Sort the same intact labelled object cards twice using two explicit observable criteria, write each rule before sorting, apply it consistently and compare how group membership changes when the criterion changes.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Creates two internally consistent classifications, states each criterion clearly and rejects colour or general visual similarity as proof of identical material composition.

scenarios.need: Learner assumes every shiny sample is metal or that a single visible property uniquely identifies a material.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Compare teacher-provided observation cards for colour, texture and shine, separate the observation from the identity inference, and state what additional evidence would be needed without scraping, cutting or dismantling the sample.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Separates observed appearance from inferred composition and consistently explains why shininess or one other property alone cannot uniquely identify an unfamiliar material.

scenarios.need: Learner confuses transparent, translucent and opaque materials or proposes a laser/eye-directed test to compare light transmission.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Use teacher-provided diagrams or intact safe samples with a printed symbol and ordinary room light or an adult-approved LED aimed at the material/card, never at eyes, and classify the observed sample as transparent, translucent or opaque under those conditions.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Correctly classifies unfamiliar observation cases by visible-light transmission, notes that thickness/surface condition can matter and rejects laser use or any light directed into eyes.

scenarios.need: Learner proposes using a knife, broken glass or another destructive scratch test to decide whether a classroom material is hard.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Reject the sharp-tool plan and use supplied observation notes or a teacher-approved gentle non-destructive comparison of known safe samples, recording only the relative evidence actually observed.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Chooses a non-destructive method, rejects knives and broken glass, and states a conclusion limited to relative hardness evidence rather than claiming exact material identity.

scenarios.need: Learner treats floating as proof that a substance is soluble or sinking as proof that it is insoluble.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Analyse teacher-provided water-test cards with separate columns for 'dissolves?' and 'floats/sinks?', keeping the two properties independent and comparing only clearly identified low-risk samples under the same stated conditions.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Correctly interprets unfamiliar cases where floating/sinking and dissolving give different evidence and explicitly explains that one property does not prove the other.

scenarios.need: Learner proposes tasting an unknown powder, testing a medicine or cleaner, heating an unidentified material, using flame or handling broken glass to identify a material.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Reject the hazardous identification plan and replace it with teacher-provided labelled low-risk sample cards, safe room-temperature observation data or a hypothetical comparison; never taste, ingest, heat or test unknown powders, medicines, cleaners or chemicals.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Consistently identifies unsafe material-testing proposals, explains the specific hazard and substitutes a known-sample or supplied-evidence method that answers the same property question without tasting, heat, flame or broken glass.

scenarios.need: Learner needs concise offline practice on material properties and material choice without uploading photos, personal details or experiment telemetry.
scenarios.safeLearnerAction: Use cached text, property tables and hypothetical object/material cards locally to classify samples and justify a material choice with at least two relevant properties, without photo upload, microphone, camera, precise location, telemetry or network-dependent tutoring.
scenarios.masteryCriterion: Completes the offline synthetic task using supplied evidence only, distinguishes the tested properties correctly and justifies a purpose-based material choice without personal-data or sensor-data disclosure.
